# Dummedhajātaka (Ja 50)

**ID:** Ja 50
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (Pali):** Dummedhajātaka

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Dummedhajātaka* (Ja 50) is the fiftieth story in the canonical Pali *Jātaka* collection, standing as the tenth and concluding discourse of the *Atthakāmavagga* and completing the first division of fifty stories (*paṭhamo paṇṇāso*) in the *Ekanipāta* [Fausböll 1877]. It shares its title with another story in the collection, Ja 122 [Fausböll 1877]. The narrative opens with the verse incipit *Dummedhānam* ("A thousand evildoers" or "unwise folk") [Fausböll 1877; Readings from the Jatakas]. According to the Nidāna framework, the Buddha related the tale while dwelling at Jetavana to illustrate conduct for the world's benefit (*lokatthacariyā*), a theme cross-referenced by the commentary to the *Mahākaṇhajātaka* of the *Dvādasanipāta* [Fausböll 1877; Readings from the Jatakas].

In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is reborn as Prince Brahmadatta in Benares [DeCaroli 2004; Fausböll 1877]. Observing crowds worshipping a banyan-tree deity (*rukkhadevatā*) with violent animal sacrifices to obtain offspring, wealth, and status, the prince determines to curb this slaughter [Appleton 2010; Sutherland 1991]. He outwardly feigns devotion to the spirit by making bloodless offerings of incense, water, and flowers [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004]. Upon ascending the throne, he proclaims that his kingship was granted by the tree deity on the condition that he sacrifice anyone who commits the five immoral actions (*pañcadussīlakammāni*), specifically animal slaughter, as an offering to the tree [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004]. Terrified by this ruse, the kingdom's subjects promptly abandon blood sacrifices and adopt moral conduct [Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth; DeCaroli 2004]. Modern scholars note that this story illustrates the Bodhisatta teaching through strategic action and didactic subterfuge [Appleton 2010], while reflecting early Buddhist efforts to reform and pacify popular spirit worship rather than eradicate it entirely [Sutherland 1991; DeCaroli 2004].
